item.title: Pakistan to open FIFA ASEAN Cup campaign against Thailand
item.description:
Pakistan start their FIFA ASEAN Cup campaign against Thailand on Sept 26 after being drawn in Group ‘B’ of Division One for the inaugural tournament, which will take place later this month with matches played in Indonesia and Hong Kong, organisers said on Thursday.

The 11 members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and three guest sides — Hong Kong, Pakistan and Bangladesh — will play in two divisions from Sept 24 .

Eight teams will contest the top-tier Division 1 — hosts Indonesia, Malaysia, Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam, Bangladesh and Pakistan .

They will be split into two sections of four with the winners contesting the first FIFA ASEAN Cup final on Oct 5 .

Pakistan have been placed in Group ‘B’ alongside Thailand, the Philippines and Vietnam .

The Green Shirts face the Philippines on Sept 29 before their final group-stage fixture against Vietnam on Oct 2.

Pakistan entered the tournament after China withdrew from the inaugural edition to focus on preparations for the 2027 Asian Cup and 2030 World Cup qualifiers.

Pakistan will enter the competition on a high after winning the Diamond Jubilee Intern­ational Football Tournament in the Maldives earlier this year, their first standalone international title since 1952.

The second-tier Division 2 will be hosted by Hong Kong and also involve Brunei, Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar and Timor-Leste, split into two three-team sections with the winners advancing to a final on Oct 3 .

“The FIFA ASEAN Cup was launched to provide national teams with meaningful competitive opportunities,” said FIFA president Gianni Infantino. “The tournament will strengthen football ties across Southeast Asia.”

item.title: CEC: No illegal instructions to police for local polls
item.description:
The Election Commission will not give any illegal instructions to the police during the upcoming local government elections, Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) AMM Nasir Uddin has said.
The CEC made the comment on Wednesday after inaugurating a training course titled “Training to Enhance the Skills and Capabilities of Police for Performing Election Duties Professionally.” The training course was inaugurated at the Rajarbagh Police Auditorium.
The chief election commissioner said: “Our commitment is total. We have sought the cooperation of the police in conducting the local government elections. The Commission has a constitutional responsibility to ensure a free and fair election, just as the police have constitutional and legal responsibilities.”
He said: “No illegal instructions will come from the Commission. They (the police) have said that they will work to ensure a credible election.”
Asked whether it would be possible to hold local government elections given the current law-and-order situation, the CEC said: “The situation is not worse now than it was during the 13th election. And we have confidence in the police. There is a political party-led government in power.”
Asked whether the police would be able to perform their election duties free from pressure, Inspector General of Police (IGP) Ali Hasan Fakir said: “There is a political party-led government now, but it is a democratic government. We will take all the measures necessary to make the election free and fair, in accordance with the Election Commission’s advice.”
Regarding efforts to restore the police’s image over the past six months, the IGP said: “I believe our success has been 100%.”

item.title: PM orders stricter action against unchecked use of polythene, plastic
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Wednesday ordered the law enforcement agencies to take stricter action to stop the unchecked use of polythene and plastic in a bid to control environmental pollution.
He also asked the ministries, departments and agencies concerned to properly discharge their responsibilities in enforcing measures against the use of polythene and plastic.
Tarique gave the directives at a review meeting on controlling environmental pollution at the Secretariat in the morning, said a release issued by the PM’s Press Wing.
The meeting discussed progress in implementing various government initiatives to control environmental pollution and future measures, including increasing the use of environment-friendly block bricks, controlling air, water, soil and noise pollution, and improving waste management.
Road Transport and Bridges, Railways and Shipping Minister Shaikh Robiul Alam, Sate Minister for Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives Mir Shahe Alam, State Minister for Water Resources Farhad Hossain Azad, State Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change Sheikh Faridul Islam, Cabinet Secretary Nasimul Ghani, Prime Minister’s Principal Secretary ABM Abdus Sattar, Dhaka South City Corporation Administrator Md Abdus Salam and Prime Minister’s Special Assistant for Environment, Forest and Climate Change Dr Saimum Parvez, among senior officials, attended the meeting.

item.title: Iran attacks US base in Jordan as Hormuz impasse deepens
item.description:
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said Wednesday they pummeled a US military base in Jordan, vowing retaliation for American strikes on Iranian oil tankers that dragged the foes deeper into war.
Tehran's bombs came after US forces destroyed five Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday in response to Iran targeting an American warship, the second such attack in less than a week.
The United States and Iran are locked in a stalemate six months into the war, with Iran maintaining a stranglehold on the Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping route for the world's oil and gas, and Washington pushing a campaign to choke Iran's ports and economy.
The Islamic Republic said on Wednesday it would target oil tankers off US-allied Kuwait and Bahrain in retaliation for the strikes on its tankers.
Minutes later, Iran's Revolutionary Guards -- the most powerful arm of the Iranian military -- said they had struck the US air base of Al-Azraq in Jordan with missiles, state media reported.
The "punitive operation" damaged maintenance and repair facilities, deployment locations and shelters for fighter jets, according to IRNA.
Jordan's army said it shot down 18 missiles from Iran targeting the kingdom.
The strikes came after Tehran urged crews on oil tankers off Kuwait and Bahrain to leave their vessels, warning they "will be targeted", the Guards said in a statement posted on IRNA.
The latest flare-up was triggered after US forces destroyed five Iranian oil tankers, with the US military saying it "directed the crews to abandon ship" before hitting the vessels.
"Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they're going to lose tankers, and I think you'll see that again today," US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters on Tuesday on a visit to Colombia.
Iranian media reported Tuesday that a US missile struck a tanker off the coast of Kharg Island, adding that there were no casualties.
The chief of staff of Iran's army Ali Abdollahi had warned the Islamic republic would hit US bases in the region if Iranian oil tankers were hit.
Global oil prices climbed on Wednesday to near $100 a barrel as the war threatened to further choke supply from the crude-rich Middle East.
The price of Brent crude, the benchmark international contract, rose to $99.38 per barrel, while the main US contract West Texas Intermediate was at $94.51 per barrel.
Iran has largely controlled the Strait of Hormuz -- which normally carries around a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas -- since the start of the war in February, with traffic through the waterway virtually paralysed.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards also said on Tuesday they seized "one of the most modern, unmanned" American submarine drone in the Strait of Hormuz.
The US military said that the drone had "malfunctioned", insisting it was an "older model" that did not carry any sensitive data.
Iranian state TV also said the Guards had attacked two US destroyers with ballistic missiles.
The US military did not immediately comment on the report.

item.title: US destroys five Iran oil tankers after attacks on American warship
item.description:
US forces destroyed five Iranian oil carriers on Tuesday after Tehran launched ballistic missiles at an American warship twice in recent days, the US military said.
The strikes are the second time Washington has targeted Iranian tankers in less than a week in response to attacks on US military vessels, and Tehran vowed to hit back by targeting oil carriers near US-allied Gulf states.
"American forces directed the crews to abandon ship before the vessels were struck and rendered inoperable," US Central Command (CENTCOM) said in a statement on the strikes, which were "in response to Iran's most recent failed attacks."
The destruction of the tankers came after "the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targeted a US Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days," CENTCOM said.
The warship "successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks and continued to patrol regional waters," it said.
US forces destroyed three Iranian crude carriers on Saturday after Iran tried to attack a US aircraft carrier and a guided missile destroyer, according to CENTCOM.
"All IRGC attempts against US Navy warships have failed," it added.
Earlier Tuesday, the chief of staff of the Iranian Armed Forces, Ali Abdollahi, had warned that Tehran would attack US bases in the region if Iranian oil tankers were hit.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio however said Washington would continue to strike them in response to Iranian attacks.
"Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they're going to lose tankers," Rubio told reporters on a visit to Colombia.
Iran said it would target tankers off US allies Kuwait and Bahrain in response to Tuesday's US strikes.
"We warn all oil tankers in the Kuwaiti and Bahraini ports... whether they are anchored or docked -- we warn them to leave their vessels because they will be targeted," according to an IRGC statement posted eon the IRNA state news agency.
CENTCOM also said Tuesday that one of its underwater drones "malfunctioned," after Iran claimed its forces captured an American unmanned submarine in the strategic Strait of Hormuz.
"An underwater drone operated by US forces malfunctioned more than a day ago. It was surveying regional waters in support of ongoing operations," CENTCOM spokesperson Captain Tim Hawkins said, without mentioning whether the device was seized by Iran.
"The defective drone was an older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment," Hawkins added.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards had said they seized a US underwater drone at the "entrance to the Strait of Hormuz in a complex intelligence and operational action," describing it as "one of the most modern, unmanned, and smart submarines" operated by US forces.

item.title: Historically strong 2026 Super El Niño could have this devastating effect on California
item.description:
A lot has been written about how this year’s Super El Niño is likely to be the strongest on record and could result in extreme weather through 2027. But we’re just learning now that it may cause serious damage to California’s coast, impacting sea levels and possibly triggering floods.

El Niño is forecast to raise sea levels along the California coast by about a foot by the middle of next month, according to oceanographer Dillon Amaya at North Carolina State University, CNN reported. That’s because the climate pattern will push water from Mexico and Central America north up to the U.S. coastline.

That may in turn trigger “Kelvin waves”—which unlike typical waves, “slosh up and down, like water in a bathtub,” where they are, in effect, stuck, according to CNN.

“Typically, we think of El Niño and its impact on precipitation, but some of the first indications that El Niño is really occurring are the arrival of these coastally trapped waves,” Amaya told CNN.

At the same time that El Niño is expected to produce those waves and higher sea levels, California is also expecting regularly occurring king tides, or “astronomically high tides,” climate scientist Daniel Swain at the University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources told American Community Media.

As a result, Swain said there is an elevated risk of coastal erosion and severe flooding around the San Francisico Bay Area, for low-lying towns and communities sitting 6 feet or less above sea level.

“El Niño doesn’t guarantee a wet winter in California,” he said. “But a very strong, potentially historically strong event, which is our expectation for this year, likely increases the amount of precipitation that California will experience this winter.”

China’s Challenge to Western Alliances
item.description:
At the 25th anniversary session of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), Chinese President Xi Jinping proposed an alternative model to Western alliances.

Mr. Xi urged developing nations and the Global South to leverage “SCO wisdom” to argue for a more equitable and orderly multipolar world and reform of global governance institutions like the United Nations. The Secretary General of the United Nations, Antonio Guterres, and other guest delegations were in attendance for this anniversary session of the SCO.

The 26th meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the SCO convened on September 1, 2026, in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan. Leaders from the 10 member states (China, Russia, India, Pakistan, Iran, and Belarus and the four Central Asian nations) signed the Bishkek Declaration and 13 other documents dealing with security, technology and anti-drug cooperation.

Mr. Xi committed China to provide localized technical projects, collaboration on Artificial Intelligence with SCO member countries and alignment through the Belt and Road initiative (BRI), a massive global and economic strategy proposed by Mr. Xi in 2013. (The BRI, with 146 member states, seeks to link Asia, Europe, Africa, and Latin America through a network of ports, railways, roads, and energy pipelines. The World Bank and other studies claim that BRI transport projects have lowered trade costs, integrated developing regions into global supply chains, increased local GDPs and lifted millions out of moderate poverty. Critics claim that aggressive, large-scale lending by Chinese state banks have saddled several developing nations with heavy external debt burdens).

Mr. Xi talks about alternatives to Western alliances and creating multipolar institutions, an appealing message to developing nations and the Global South.

It is ironic, however, that two of the 10 members of the SCO, Russia and Iran, are pariah states. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, despite security guarantees provided to Ukraine after they sent all their nuclear warheads to Russia; and Iran, a state sponsor of terrorism that, in 1999, 2009, 2019, 2022, and 2026, killed thousands of peaceful protesters.

A new alliance between Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan – the Mecca Defense Alliance – was established in August 2026. Indeed, this is an unprecedented alliance of three U.S. allies’ intent on building a security architecture independent of the U.S.

The BRICS (Brazil, Rusia, India China, and South Africa), formed in 2006, has 11 members, with more than 30 countries that either applied or expressed interest in becoming a member.

It appears that Mr. Xi’s exhortations for a more multipolar war resonates with several developing countries and the Global South, despite the inclusion of Russia and Iran in the SCO and BRICS.

Mr. Xi is competing with several U.S. led international organizations: the QUAD (Australia, India, Japan and the U.S.), AUKUS (Australia, the United Kingdom, and the U.S.), and NATO. Indeed, NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organization) was established in April 1949. It’s mission: to safeguard the freedom and security of all 32 member countries through diplomacy and military means. Article 5 of the NATO charter is clear: An armed attack against one member is considered an attack against all of them.

Any real or perceived tension between the U.S. and member countries within NATO, the QUAD or AUKUS will make Mr. Xi’s efforts to create “an orderly multipolar world”, with China in the lead, more attractive to developing countries and the Global South.

The U.S. has played a global leadership role after World War II. The Marshall Plan, established by the U.S. in 1948, provided $13 billion to help rebuild Western European economies.

And it was U.S. leadership in 1949 that established NATO.

Our allies and partners continue to look to the U.S. for this type of global leadership. And developing countries and the Global South should be looking to the U.S. as the democratic leader they should emulate and work with.

item.title: Russia’s AI Blueprint Exposes an Authoritarian Playbook
item.description:
Russia, China, and Iran are all sharing the same playbook for corrupting Western elections. The United States is on track to be the next target this November.

A troveof Russian documents leaked in May outlines Moscow’s plans to use AI to warp foreign decision-making and sway elections. The Kremlin’s “Projects 2026” strategy reveals Russia’s plot to influence upcoming elections in Europe and Israel. Their tactics are similar to those used by China and Iran for years, and what emerges isn’t a Russian innovation — it’s a shared authoritarian playbook.

Projects 2026 calls for the creation of an opinion leader database to monitor the social media profiles of 10,000 influential individuals across Europe, including the 100 most prominent opposition figures in France alone. This is precisely the model Chinese state-aligned company GoLaxy piloted against the United States in 2025. The firm reportedly built constantly evolving psychological profiles of 117 members of Congress and roughly 2,000 additional American opinion leaders.

Researchers at Vanderbilt University warned that GoLaxy appeared prepared to target these individuals with messaging aligned with Beijing’s priorities. By monitoring the social media profiles of Western leaders, China and Russia are able to map the target’s values, beliefs, emotional tendencies, and vulnerabilities, making their influence operations more tailored and impactful.

In addition to using AI to build psychological profiles, the authoritarian playbook calls for countries like Russia and Iran to flood their targets with tailored generative AI content. Projects 2026’s “AI News” initiative calls for producing more than 500 short videos to target French audiences across six social media platforms. This tactic mirrors Iranian information operations during the 2025 and 2026 wars with Israel and the United States, when pro-Iranian networks pushed AI-generated and AI-assisted videos tailored to different audiences across X and TikTok, which racked up millions of views. These countries are running highly productive propaganda engines.

The most durable piece of Projects 2026 isn’t the content at all — it’s the plan to create fictitious think tanks and research institutes that can hand Russian narratives a “legitimate information source,” making them more likely to be cited by real news outlets and large language models. The leak shows this already underway: A site called the “World Center for Strategic Studies,” registered in March 2026, published unsigned analysis aimed at Western think tank audiences, with versions planned in German, French, and Spanish. The fake think tank doesn’t need to fool a discerning reader. It needs to get quoted, indexed permanently, and cited by the next AI model that goes looking for sources on the topic.

Iran ran a cruder version of this same play: Iranian state-sponsored cyber espionage groups have repeatedly impersonated real institutions — such as the Royal United Services Institute, the Aspen Institute, and the Washington Institute — to steal credentials and plant material under a trusted name. Projects 2026 proposes something more sustainable: Don’t just hijack existing credibility but manufacture new institutions and let them accrue it over time.

Projects 2026 also proposes building a real Israel-based research institute staffed by Israeli citizens with genuine academic credentials. This approach is reminiscent of the 2014 “Iran Expert Initiative,” where Iranian Foreign Ministry officials attempted to court and influence Western think tank researchers to promote their perspectives and give them legitimacy. Emails leaked in 2023 showed that Iranian diplomats had worked with Western experts across 10 think tanks to aggressively tout the merits of the 2015 nuclear deal between Tehran and major world powers, formally known as the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action.

In the age of AI, influencing think tanks is narrative laundering at its most dangerous. Once a fabricated or state-aligned source gets cited by a legitimate outlet or indexed by a search engine, it can become part of the training and retrieval corpus that AI systems draw upon.

While the plays are reusable, the targets are new, and for Russia, the target is European elections.

The leaked documents outline a plan to swing Armenia’s parliamentary vote through a Russian-diaspora outlet and a “Mitteleuropa” initiative aimed at reshaping alignments in Hungary and Slovakia. This is where the surveillance, flooding, and laundering modules converge. To counter it, policy solutions must be swift and targeted.

First, allied governments should require disclosure of foreign funding and foreign state links for any media outlet, think tank, or “research institute” operating ahead of an election in an at-risk state — closing exactly the gap that lets a “World Center for Strategic Studies” pass as domestic and independent. Research by the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD) into Qatari money in American higher education shows what a real transparency regimen requires: disclosures reaching individual researchers, not just institutions; low reporting thresholds with real penalties; registration in the style of the Foreign Agents Registration Act for state-directed “institutes” masquerading as independent organizations; and provisions against the kind of obstruction Qatar used to block Texas A&M’s funding records in court. Russia is proposing to build the same laundering vehicle in Europe that Gulf money has already normalized in American academia. The fix already exists — it just needs to be strengthened.

Second, platforms should both demonetize and remove unlabeled AI-generated political content during designated pre-election windows in at-risk states. X’s own emergency policy during the Iran war, which suspended digital influencers’ ability to monetize their content for 90 days on undisclosed AI-generated war footage, shows platforms already have the infrastructure to act fast when the stakes are high enough. But demonetization alone left the content up and circulating; independent researchers found AI-generated war footage kept flooding feeds regardless of the policy. Elections warrant a harder line: If posts feature undisclosed AI-generated content during an active election period, they shouldn’t just lose ad revenue. They should come down.

Third, Washington should prepare for future attempts at election influence by boosting the protection mechanisms it already has in place. Currently, 31 states have passed election deepfake laws, but they are under legal scrutiny because they touch on domestic speech. Federal action targeting foreign actors rests on firm ground. The 2002 McCain-Feingold Act prevents electioneering communications by foreign actors, but this only applies to broadcast, cable, and satellite communications. It must be updated to explicitly include paid internet and digital advertisements. It should also close the gap on AI-generated political content and require labeling so that foreign deepfakes can’t hide behind current ambiguities.

Projects 2026 is not evidence that Russia has cracked something new. It’s evidence that Moscow, Beijing, and Tehran are now running the same AI playbook against the same democracies, taking turns testing which module works best. The future outlined in Projects 2026 may not be here yet, but objects in the mirror are closer than they appear.

item.title: Lawmakers reach for AI legislation after researchers warn of extinction
item.description:
Welcome to AI Decoded, Fast Company‘s weekly newsletter that breaks down the most important news in the world of AI. I’m Mark Sullivan, a senior writer at Fast Company, covering emerging tech, AI, and tech policy.

Sign up to receive this newsletter every week via email here. And if you have comments on this issue and/or ideas for future ones, drop me a line at sullivan@fastcompany.com, and follow me on X @thesullivan.

“It’s time to sound the alarm”

The resignation of the Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, and his statements afterward, have sent shock waves through the AI community. Coxon, who left the company on Tuesday, tweeted that he spent the last three years working on model pretraining research at both Anthropic and OpenAI, and that the people building the models “earnestly believe it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” “They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon wrote. His post has been viewed more than 70 million times. The resignation follows incidents in which artificial intelligence agents broke out of their sandboxes, accessed the internet, and broke into other companies’ servers.

Now the shock waves have moved into political circles; a number of high-profile figures are calling for an immediate halt to frontier model research.

The Illinois governor, JB Pritzker, a Democrat, referenced Coxon’s resignation and called for industry and federal action:

“It’s time to sound the alarm – louder – on reining in Artificial Intelligence. It’s becoming more clear the threat AI poses to humanity, so I’m calling for immediate action from the industry and Washington.”

In a follow-up post, Pritzker called for an end to big tech lobbying against safety rules and for congressional hearings on AI development. “When AI researchers are whistleblowing, we need to listen,” he wrote. “They are telling us this technology could be as dangerous as a nuclear bomb.”

Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for a U.S. Senate seat in Michigan, quoted the same Coxon thread:

“Most tech geeks don’t resign from their roles because . . . the tech they’re building could end humanity. How we change the incentives leading AI labs down this path and protect against these existential risks are defining political questions of our time.”

Later the same day, he posted a video: “AI development is moving faster than our ability to assure its safety. It’s time to hit pause until we can assure it won’t . . . destroy us.”

Chris Van Hollen, U.S. senator from Maryland and also a Democrat, quoted Coxon and called both for slowing AI research and for new regulations:

“Anyone still denying the risks posed by unregulated AI should read this thread. It’s time to pump the brakes & take action NOW. We need: Mandatory safeguards; A comprehensive testing regime; Urgent dialogue with China, before & during President Xi’s visit to DC this month.”

U.S. Representative Pat Ryan, a New York Democrat, called for better “pacing” of AI research:

“1) We need emergency hearings on pacing the frontier – NOW!! 2) This November, we need to elect leaders willing to stand up to AI oligarchs and fight for the American people.”

After news that OpenAI agents had broken into Hugging Face servers, Ryan tweeted:

“When I wrote a letter with [Texas Democratic representative Greg Casar] to OpenAI last month (post Hugging Face), we asked whether other similar incidents had occurred. They refused to tell us. Then this comes out. The House Democratic Majority arrives in January. I look forward to the public hearings.”

Evan Hubinger, alignment science team lead at Anthropic, tweeted in support of Coxon’s views. “I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to,” he wrote.

Samuel Marks, who runs Anthropic’s scalable oversight division, wrote in a personal capacity that developers continue building despite the risk of human extinction because of commercial incentives and a belief that they are racing less responsible competitors, Variety reported.

Bernie Sanders, the independent U.S. senator from Vermont, wrote Wednesday that “Mr. Coxon is right” and said he will introduce legislation to ban superintelligence and pause AI development, Forbes reported. The Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act would halt development of AI systems capable of surpassing human intelligence and impose a temporary pause on other advanced systems until a new federal regulator sets safety rules.

U.S. representatives Greg Casar, a Texas Democrat; Lori Trahan, a Massachusetts Democrat; and Anna Paulina Luna, a Florida Republican, along with Governor Ron DeSantis of Florida, a Republican, and the former presidential candidate Andrew Yang have also responded to Coxon’s resignation, sounding the alarm about out-of-control AI development.

The Trump administration, meanwhile, has generally pushed to accelerate AI development while reducing what it considers burdensome regulation.

U.S. agencies accuse 6 Chinese AI companies of industrial-scale model copying

The National Security Agency, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, and the FBI issued a joint advisory Tuesday accusing Chinese AI companies of extracting the proprietary functionalities and capabilities of American frontier models, Engadget reported. The advisory names DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Alibaba, MiniMax, StepFun, and Z.AI, and says they took billions of tokens across millions of exchanges from Anthropic’s Claude, OpenAI’s GPT, Google’s Gemini, and xAI’s Grok since at least late 2024. The agencies said the practice is tacitly encouraged but not directed by political leaders in Beijing, and that distillation is the critical core of these firms’ development rather than a supplement.

OpenAI says 10,000 agents solved a Millennium Prize problem

OpenAI published a proposed solution to the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of seven Millennium Prize Problems set by the Clay Mathematics Institute, each carrying a $1 million award. OpenAI says roughly 10,000 agents running on an unreleased internal model reached the result on September 5, about 88 hours after the first agents launched, exchanging 2.7 million messages and generating about 130 billion output tokens. Checking and formalizing the proof took another 17 hours using GPT-6 Astra.

Suno launches models trained on licensed music

Suno released a new generation of music models that it developed with Warner Music Group, BMG, and Believe, Jack Brody, Suno’s chief product officer, told Axios. They’re the first models Suno has built under its music industry partnerships, and the company still blocks users from prompting it to make a song in the likeness of a known artist or song. Reportedly, Suno will retire its previous models, a portion of revenue will be shared with the partners from launch day, and rights holders are responsible for distributing that money. 

Mistral raises 3 billion euros, Europe’s largest private tech round

The European AI lab Mistral AI raised 3 billion euros (almost $3.5 billion) at a post-money valuation above 21 billion euros, which the company describes as the largest equity fundraising round ever completed by a European technology company. Samsung Electronics led the round with Scaleup Europe Fund and an existing investor, PSG Equity. TechCrunch reported that new backers include Advent and BlackRock, that existing backers a16z, Nvidia, and Salesforce Ventures participated, and that the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg joined as a new investor. Mistral says it will use the money to expand frontier research, scale compute capacity for training, and grow internationally.

Google will spend 13 billion euros on Finnish data centers

Google said Wednesday it will invest at least 13 billion euros ($15.1 billion) in AI infrastructure in Finland, its largest single investment in Europe, CNBC reported. Bloomberg reported the money will go toward at least three new data centers plus an expansion of the company’s existing site in Hamina over the next two years. In its own announcement, Google says the investment includes clean energy projects and community funds.

item.title: Trump’s clash with Canada is his latest imperialistic embarrassment | Sidney Blumenthal
item.description:
The president’s chaotic schemes of aggrandizement, from Venezuela to Iran, have no larger rationale

Trumpism is the lowest stage of imperialism. “We’re not going to invade Greenland. We’re going to buy it,” Donald Trump reportedly told the annual black-tie dinner on 1 February of the private Alfalfa Club, an assemblage of prominent Washington figures, a number of whom he had publicly humiliated, and others he was investigating or suing. “It’s never been my intention to make Greenland the 51st state. I want to make Canada the 51st state. Greenland will be the 52nd state. Venezuela can be 53rd.” The room greeted several of his remarks with dead silence. His cosplay as the Pirate King was not received as a good-humored takeoff from a Gilbert and Sullivan opera. He went on. “So many people in the room I hate,” he said in a display of honesty. “Most of you I like,” he claimed. Then, at his peak euphoria, he flew off to Mar-a-Lago to plan his attack on Iran, which took place 27 days later.

Trump’s imperialism of piracy and plunder is less of a system even than that of the earliest imperialism of 17th century privateers raiding the Spanish Main, the divine right of kings, and monarchs dividing up the spoils as favors to create their lords and earls. His schemes of aggrandizement operating by threat and force are justified by no larger rationale, nothing as exalted as “the white man’s burden”, marauding wherever and however he can to seize resources.

25 years after 9/11. Whatever happened to mass-effect terrorism?
item.description:
One remaining mystery about 9/11 is why there have been no attacks of comparable scale since. But, with the combination of new motivations, enhanced means of delivery and AI -devised payloads there should be no cause for complacency.

9/11 changed everything. It led to two decades when the United States and much of Europe became fixated on Islamism. Western strategists became fluent about half absorbed subjects such as Wahhabism, Pashtun tribal customs, Frontier Crimes Regulations, and the Anbar Awakening while giving insufficient attention to Chinese economic dominance and Russian military rearmament[1]. Who knows what that diversion of strategic and intellectual resources (and the chaos it left behind in the region) has cost the West?

9/11 also bookends that remarkable period from the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1989/90 when peace and reconciliation seemed to break out everywhere. The Oslo Accords of 1993 seemed to chart a trajectory towards a two-state solution in Israel/Palestine. One year later the peaceful multi-party elections in South Africa were nothing short of a miracle. For years Afrikaners had insisted they would fight black rule until the last drop of white blood. This was the brief ‘unipolar moment’ under the (then) benign supervision of Washington.

9/11 ushered in a new world; one with which Thomas Hobbes would be all too familiar. “Covenants, without the sword, are but words and of no strength to secure a man at all.” “Force and fraud are in war the two cardinal virtues.” Leviathan could be quoted endlessly. .[2]

Of course, first and foremost, 9/11was a tragedy for the victims and their families. It was an act of appalling savagery. It was not only the largest terrorist attack in history by a country mile but it also introduced a new concept of mass-effect terrorism.

From the terrorists’ point of view it was also an attack of breathtaking scale and ambition. Osama Bin Laden had the imagination to view an aircraft full of fuel and passengers as a terror weapon by knitting together two of Al Qaida’s (AQ) previous failures; the truck-bomb attack on the World Trade Centre in 1993 and the 1995 Operation BOJINKA in the Philippines. Both attacks had been planned by Ramzi Yousef whose uncle Khalid Sheikh Mohammed was the chief planner for 9/11.

It was also, from an AQ viewpoint, both triumphant and disastrous. Its success was that a superpower overreacted for two decades and allowed 9/11 to shape the whole of Western foreign policy as a Global War on Terror (GWOT). Its failure was due to Washington’s largely successful determination to destroy AQ, a success which was only imperilled when President Trump approved the feckless Doha Accords with the Taliban in 2020 opening the way to the return of AQ to Afghanistan the following year. The latest United Nations report on terrorism confirms that AQ continues to reestablish itself.[3]

As early as 1998 the British government had warned Washington that it was the likely next target in an operation which would involve hijacked aircraft. This story was told in detail by RUSI for the twentieth anniversary of 9/11.[4] The intelligence was briefed to both Presidents Clinton and Bush (junior). Contrary to widespread opinion the concept of mass-effect terrorism had been exercising minds in Washington and Whitehall long before 9/11. If they had not made the intellectual leap of imagining airliners as weapons, they had nonetheless been thinking a great deal about mass casualty attacks. This was prompted by three convergent factors.

First, in Tokyo a doomsday cult known as Aum Shinrikyo had, in 1995, released sarin on the Tokyo metro in an attack which (had it been carried out more effectively) could have killed thousands. This led to much discussion of how to react to a similar attack on the London Underground. There was also concern about CBW elements being brought into the country inside the diplomatic mail bags of state sponsors of terrorism (the bags being protected from scrutiny by the Vienna Convention of 1961).[5]

Secondly there were fears at the time about Al Qaida getting its hands on nuclear material and producing a dirty bomb (not a nuclear explosion). At the time it was believed that fissile material was being sold by former employees of Soviet nuclear programme and finding its way through Central Asia to Pakistan. Most of it was a scam called ‘red mercury’ which was thoroughly investigated at the time but there were enough more credible reports to create uncertainty[6].

And finally it was known that AQ had two scientists working on CBN (chemical, biological and nuclear) experiments out of Derunta camp near the Afghan/Pakistan border. Not all the fine detail was known but one of the scientists, Dr. Sultan Bashiruddin Mahmood, had previously worked on Pakistan’s own sovereign nuclear programme. This story was well-told a decade later by the veteran journalist Peter Bergen[7].

Thus began a decade long United States fixation with the danger of terrorists obtaining access to Pakistan’s nuclear weapons. President Obama insisted that ‘The single biggest threat to U.S. security, both short term, medium term and long term, would be the possibility of a terrorist organization obtaining a nuclear weapon.’[8]

Once 9/11 had happened the assumption was that there would be numerous copy-cat attacks. In London much focus was devoted to the towers at Canary Wharf which housed some of the world’s premier financial institutions and which were also close to the flight paths of both London Heathrow and London City airport.

In the years immediately after 9/11 terrorist ambitions remained high including the Bali bombing in 2002 (202 killed), the Madrid train bombings in 2004 (193) and London 2005 (52). There were some dangerous plots in UK notably CREVICE in 2003 and RHYME in 2004 but the only one on the scale of 9/11 was Operation OVERT in 2006, AQ’s plan to bring down seven airliners in mid Atlantic. Fortunately it was thwarted by MI5.

And herein lies the real mystery. There have been numerous nasty and costly terrorist attacks since but none on the 9/11 scale. There is a danger of sounding callous when observing that none of Mumbai in 2008 (166 killed), Paris in 2015 (130), Sri Lanka 2019 (269) come even close to 9/11 (2,976).[9]

Two types of terrorism have emerged since OVERT in 2006.

The first was ‘urban siege’, ‘swarm’ or ‘rampaging’ terrorism which we first saw at Mumbai in 2008[10] and the Westgate shopping mall in Nairobi in 2013 (which killed 71). This is an effective form of terrorism because it captures press attention for hours (62 hours in the case of Mumbai) and makes prompt armed response extremely difficult. However it is also costly for the terrorists who are nearly always killed or captured and their supporting organisations and states identified. The Indians were relentlessly successful in following up the Mumbai attack although the Lashkar-e-Tayyiba still exists and represent a significant threat to regional peace.[11]

The second (and now the most common) is ‘lone wolf’ terrorism committed usually by lone (and lonely) young men who have become self-radicalised online in their bedrooms and take the family car or a kitchen knife and seek to kill as many people as possible. The problem with this second type is that it is almost indistinguishable from wider mental health problems brought about by social isolation. It risks a substantial drain on the precious resources of security services which need to be focussing on strategic threats (such as those posed by Russia, Iran and China as well as terrorist groups).

In terms of mass casualties only one is comparable with 9/11; the brutal Hamas incursion into southern Israel on 7th October 2023. As a proportion of Israel’s population it is probably the most lethal terrorist attack in history. But there the comparison ends. The attack involved guns, knives and grenades; a far cry from the use of aircraft as a weapon against a ground-based target.

Aircraft and their passengers have often been targets before, notably PanAm 103 at Lockerbie in 1988 (270 deaths), UTA flight 772 the following year over Niger (170) and the often-forgotten Air India flight 182 off the Irish coast in 1985 (329)[12]. But in each case the aircraft and passengers were the target rather than the means of delivery against an objective on the ground. 25 years after 9/11 one would have expected to have seen several similar attacks using aircraft against buildings or (even worse) against stadiums full of spectators.

Why has this not happened?

Precautions taken by airlines should take some credit. Cockpit doors have been strengthened and protocols have been largely enforced although there are signs of laxness creeping back in.

Security services have used bulk data to identify suspicious trends and plots early. Artificial Intelligence will help here. It is now much harder for terrorists to operate as groups.

And the US military, their intelligence services and allies wreaked considerable damage on both AQ and Islamic State (IS) from 2001 through until 2019.

So was 9/11 a one off rather than (as we feared) the start of a new trend? It is still too early to say. Motivation for terrorism remains strong (especially following the destruction of Gaza since October 2023). The advances in drone technology in Ukraine since 2022 could provide terrorists with an effective means of delivery at a time when counter-measures are still in their infancy. And AI could enable terrorists to research and develop lethal payloads.

As we remember 9/11 it is still too early to elcome the absence of a successful repeat during that costly quarter century. [13]

item.title: The Battle for Decision Autonomy, The New Front in Strategic Competition
item.description:
This is the talk Dave Pitts gave at the Sarajevo Security Conference in September 2026, which was based on the talk presented at the Cognitive Security Institute Conference in August 2026. Dave has identified Decision Autonomy as a key battle in the cognitive domain and a new front in strategic competition.

In 2022, Russia expected Ukraine’s political leadership to fracture in the face of pervasive disinformation, subversion, efforts to decapitate the government and to persuade Russian-speaking Ukrainians to support Russia. It expected fear, confusion, and chaos to result in surrender, flight, or capitulation. There was one problem—Ukraine resisted.

President Zelensky's refusal to flee, combined with unified military and civilian resistance—critical decisions—enabled Ukraine to hold in those critical early hours and days. How did such a small number of people resist such extraordinary pressure and make such consequential decisions?

In 2024, a mature Russian plot to assassinate Armin Papperger, CEO of Rheinmetall, a major producer of artillery shells for Ukraine, was discovered and disrupted by German and Western intelligence. More recently, German reporting described a suspected Russian-linked plot against Stefan Thumann of Donaustahl, a German drone producer supporting Ukraine.

What could those plots have achieved if successful? What did they actually achieve?

Russian drone incursions, airspace violations, political interference, cyberattacks, undersea cable cutting, GPS jamming, forced migration, sabotage, assassination, and attacks on critical infrastructure—several things have become increasingly clear. Russia’s gray zone attacks have increased since it invaded Ukraine. They have become more brazen, more lethal and more destructive—and spread across an increasing number of European countries.

The real question behind these attacks is why Russia is doing this. There are some obvious answers, but do we have it right?

America directly—and many countries indirectly—face a strategic challenge in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran’s attempts to control the flow of vital global energy as leverage in its conflict with the United States and Israel have created a wicked strategic decision point. Iran’s concurrent attacks on its neighbors may also serve as decision accelerants, compressing the time available to assess options and increasing pressure to act.

What decisions are possible and potentially effective? What are the risks and consequences of each option? And, perhaps most importantly, how much influence over that decision does Iran have?

No single human capacity is more powerful—or more vulnerable—than the ability to make decisions. Throughout history and continuing today, human decision-making has remained a target of those who seek to control the choices of others.

The ability—and the autonomy—to make decisions, from the ordinary choices of everyday life to the most consequential decisions of war and peace, makes us uniquely human. We instinctively resist—and, if necessary, fight—as individuals, groups, and nations when others seek to control our choices, think for us, or suppress this core human capacity.

At first glance, these stories seem completely unrelated.

A President fighting for his nation’s survival
Targeted assassinations of defense executives
Sabotage across the cities of Europe
A high-stakes standoff in the Strait of Hormuz.

They aren't.

They're four stories about the same thing: Decision autonomy. Different actors. Different circumstances. Different outcomes. One framework.

What is Decision Autonomy?

Decision Autonomy is our individual and collective ability to accurately see the world around us, to trust the knowledge we have and the information we receive, and to make independent, confident decisions based on our own judgment. “I decide—we decide.” To be clear, this is about all of us—citizens, private sector leaders, military commanders and officials, and policymakers.

It’s not a perfect state, it isn’t binary, and it exists on a spectrum. Individuals, organizations, and nations are constantly moving along this spectrum—sometimes toward greater autonomy, and sometimes toward greater vulnerability to external pressure.

In the middle of that spectrum is Decision Malleability—a state in which decision autonomy becomes increasingly susceptible to external influences. We see reality less clearly, cognitive clarity erodes, judgment is increasingly influenced, and decisions are increasingly shaped by external pressures.

At the far end of that spectrum is Decision Compromise—a state in which external influences have displaced or constrained independent judgment, resulting in the loss of decision autonomy. Reality is distorted, cognitive clarity is lost, independent judgment is displaced, and decisions are no longer fully your own.

Our adversaries understand this. They don't have to completely compromise our decision-making to succeed. They simply have to move us toward greater decision malleability—just enough to delay a decision, divide an organization, increase uncertainty, create hesitation, or influence a false choice.

If we accept that the ultimate objective of cognitive warfare is to undermine, degrade, and compromise decision autonomy, then understanding what our adversaries are doing to achieve that goal is important. This battle—the battle for Decision Autonomy—is becoming the new front in strategic competition.

What external pressures are our adversaries using in this battle? There are many, but I want to focus on four primary pathways.

First—deception. Deception distorts our understanding of the world around us—reality itself—by persuading us that false realities are real, to doubt the truth we actually see, or simply misperceive the environment in which we are making decisions. What does deception sound like?

“Ukraine is run by Nazis.”

“We are not attacking you—we are protecting you.”

“They started it.”

“Joining NATO would be a hostile act.”

Second—manipulation. Manipulation influences our judgment by exploiting our emotions, identities, biases, and motivations, steering how we evaluate information and the decisions we make. Fear, anger, exhaustion, hopelessness, or hope can override deliberate reasoning. What does manipulation sound like?

“The West doesn’t respect who you are.”

“America will abandon you.”

“China offers a future that NATO can’t.”

“Why should those from outside the region tell you how to run your country?”

Third—coercion. Coercion constrains our freedom to choose by threatening or imposing unacceptable consequences if we do not make the decision our adversaries desire. The logic is simple: “you do X and we’ll respond forcefully.” What does coercion sound like?

“Join and we will take action.”

“Recognize Taiwan and there will be consequences.”

“Support our enemies and your interests will not be safe.”

“Advance our interests in the region or lose access to our markets.”

Fourth—cognitive overload. Cognitive overload overwhelms our ability to think clearly and rationally by exceeding our capacity to process information, evaluate competing narratives, and anticipate the consequences of our decisions. What does cognitive overload feel like?

“An endless stream of conflicting narratives.”

“One video says one thing—another says the opposite.”

“Experts disagree.”

“Anonymous sources contradict official sources.”

“Too many decisions, too much information, too little certainty, too little time.”

Our adversaries seek to create cognitive overload; our objective is to preserve cognitive clarity.

Cognitive clarity isn’t merely the absence of confusion. It’s the ability to remain intellectually focused, emotionally composed, and deliberately engaged despite uncertainty, complexity, competing information, information overload, and attempts to shape judgment.

In terms of these decision states, let’s test the framework against the five examples I opened with.

In Ukraine, President Zelensky and Ukraine maintained decision autonomy. They held firmly to reality, resisted deception, manipulation, and coercion, and made independent decisions despite extraordinary pressure. In this case, decision autonomy prevailed.

Russia’s assassination plots failed to remove key decision makers or undermine support for Ukraine. In fact, exposure of the plots appears to have had the opposite effect—hardening political resolve, increasing intelligence collaboration, strengthening protective measures around critical industrial leaders, and prompting defense companies to increase production. In this case, exposing Russia’s deception sharpened the view of reality and strengthened decision autonomy rather than degrading it.

Russia’s sabotage campaign has been heavy and costly. It is hard to assess if decision autonomy has been degraded. What is clear is that shared operational awareness has increased, defense collaboration is on the rise, an awareness that Russia favors Endless Warfare over peace is settling in, and a goal of shared strategic deterrence has emerged. If there’s a lesson here, it’s that an adversary can create enormous pressure without necessarily achieving decision compromise.

Iran’s disruption of the Strait of Hormuz has revealed the limitations of conventional military power against an adversary employing gray and asymmetric warfare methods. More importantly, it demonstrates how even a superpower finds its decision space constrained by a committed adversary.

The U.S. and its allies are moving along the decision continuum as they seek a decision to resolve this crisis. The question is whether this movement along the continuum reflects normal strategic decision-making under pressure—or a degradation of decision autonomy.

All these examples identify five key points that can protect decision autonomy:

Protect reality.
Seek evidence. Challenge assumptions. Verify before believing.

Preserve independent judgment.
Don't outsource your thinking to algorithms, echo chambers, crowds, or even experts that speak at conferences.

Maintain cognitive clarity.
Slow down. Reduce noise. Watch for fatigue, anger, urgency, despair, and overload.

Recognize and resist coercion.
“Am I choosing this—or am I being pressured into it?”

Continuously assess your decision autonomy.
Where am I on the continuum right now—autonomy, malleability, or compromise?

Is this relevant to the great power competition we all play a role in today?

Imagine these same pathways—deception, manipulation, coercion, and cognitive overload—employed deliberately and systematically by our adversaries over years or even decades, supported by intelligence services, state media, proxies, cyber capabilities, artificial intelligence, economic leverage, and military power. Scale changes everything.

Let’s talk about Russia, China, and Iran. All three countries use all four pathways, but each tends to emphasize them differently.

Russia has increasingly adopted a strategy of persistent confrontation with the West. It recognizes that it cannot match the United States, NATO, and its allies across every dimension of national power, so it competes asymmetrically and in the Gray Zone.

Russia seeks advantage by increasing uncertainty, delaying decisions, dividing alliances, employing proxies, and raising the perceived costs of action. It exploits negotiations to shift blame, abruptly change positions, and weaponize deception, delay, and distraction.

Russia understands that it doesn't have to defeat its adversaries militarily if it can influence their decisions before military force is ever employed. Deception and coercion define its approach.

Deception through disinformation, false narratives, active measures, and reflexive control.

Coercion through nuclear signaling, red lines, energy leverage, sabotage, assassination, and intimidation.

For China, patience is a strategic weapon. Rather than seeking to influence a single decision, China seeks to shape the long-term decision environment so that decisions favorable to Beijing gradually become the norm and ultimately viewed as being in the target's own interest.

As leading foreign policy expert Elizabeth Economy has observed, “China is executing a patient, multi-decade campaign to dominate the "new frontiers of power"—a continuous effort to set conditions, rewrite rules, and erode Western advantages below the threshold of open conflict.

Manipulation and coercion define this approach.”

Manipulation through United Front activities, influence operations, elite networks, and weaponized narratives.

Coercion through economic leverage, market access, technology dependence, sanctions, military expansion, and aggressive maritime tactics.

Iran views its struggle against the West as enduring and existential. Rather than seeking decisive military victory against stronger powers, it relies on persistent gray-zone competition, asymmetric warfare, and proxies to preserve regime security while constraining the decision of its adversaries.

Iran seeks to narrow the choices of the U.S. and its regional allies—"accommodate its interests or accept an unending and costly regional conflict.”

Manipulation and coercion define its approach.

Manipulation through ideological narratives, proxy media, and the exploitation of political divisions, sectarian identities, and regional instability.

Coercion through threats to global energy supplies, proxy violence, direct attacks on neighbors, hostage-taking, and terrorism.

Although their approaches differ, all three share a common objective: to shape how we perceive reality, exercise judgment, and ultimately make decisions that advance their interests over our own.

Of course, our adversaries still try to shape specific beliefs, but the longer-term payoff comes from shaping the conditions under which those beliefs form—to keep us consistently closer to Decision Malleability on issues most important to them.

So, what do we do about it? Let me close with what I believe are the human foundations of cognitive security—protecting cognition and decision autonomy.

This is often where we start talking about structural fixes—new organizations, whole-of-government approaches, media literacy, and technology. Some may be necessary; some remain aspirational. But I'd like to leave that conversation for another day and focus on the more human side of cognitive security: protecting cognition and decision autonomy.

Today, a clear view of reality can resemble a wilderness of mirrors—seeing isn't believing. If adversaries can replace facts with disinformation and synthetic realities, they gain a decision advantage.

Most of us have too many sources of information flooding our professional and private lives—I certainly do. It is easy to rely on so-called experts, chatbots, social media, comfortable echo chambers, and ubiquitous algorithms to do our thinking for us. It can become a blissful rut. When we knowingly or unknowingly cede judgment and decision space to others—we begin to lose decision autonomy.

We are living in a cognitive storm—a chaotic and unreliable global information environment where a single operator with a laptop can reach millions at the speed of global communications, where countless media sources are almost impossible to vet in real time, and where adversaries deploy AI-enabled networks of surrogates, fake sites, cybercriminals, hacktivists, and bots to target all of us and our institutions. It is easy to feel overwhelmed.

Russia, China, Iran, and even North Korea use redlines, threats and intimidation as tools of persuasion. The fear of escalation can be powerful, and our adversaries will seek to use coercion to move us along the continuum toward malleability and compromise. Coercion changes how we see the cost of our decisions and what we are willing to risk.

Our goal is to recognize coercion for what it is and not allow the fear of consequences—real or manufactured—to become the basis for our decisions.

We do have to accept certain things.

We cannot eliminate deception.

We cannot eliminate manipulation.

We cannot eliminate coercion.

We cannot eliminate cognitive overload.

But before making our most consequential decisions—in a military command post, a policy meeting, during a crisis, or in negotiations with our adversaries—we can stop—and ask four questions. I call this the Decision Autonomy Diagnostic: four questions to instantly evaluate where you stand on the continuum.

Do I accurately see and understand the world around me?

or - Do I know what’s true?

Am I evaluating the information objectively, or is something shaping my judgment?

or - Can I recognize manipulation?

Have I preserved cognitive clarity despite uncertainty, complexity, and overload?

or- Can I still think and deliberate clearly?

Can I decide independently despite external pressures?

or - Can I resist false threats and real pressure?

Finally, decision autonomy is ultimately about sovereignty. For nations, sovereignty is the freedom to determine their own future without external influence or interference—self-determination.

For individuals, decision autonomy is the expression of that same principle—personal sovereignty—the freedom to see reality clearly, exercise independent judgment, and make decisions that remain our own. Sovereignty gives us the right to decide. Decision Autonomy gives us the ability to decide.

No human capacity is more powerful—or more vulnerable—than our ability to make decisions—as individuals, as people, as nations—together, we must go to great lengths to protect it.

Can 'America First' survive Trump's war-first presidency?
item.description:
In a Thursday address at the GOP midterm convention that exalted President Donald Trump and demeaned his opponents as “extremists who openly hate our nation,” Vice President JD Vance hardly spoke about foreign policy.

He did not mention the war in Iran directly, and he only brought up foreign policy as an example of an issue that divides the party’s base. He urged voters not to “throw the baby out with the bathwater” because “you happen to disagree with us on a policy issue here or there.”

The acknowledgement of foreign policy as a divisive issue in the MAGA coalition is a stark retreat for Vance, who staked his 2023 endorsement of Trump on the fact that “he started no wars despite enormous pressure from his own party and even members of his own administration,” framing the president’s America First record as a much-needed deviation from decades of bipartisan hawkishness.

A few wars later, Vance appears to have backed down from the anti-war aspects of the America First movement. Meanwhile, in response to the Iran war and the administration’s supposed betrayal of its campaign promises, the Institute for Peace & Diplomacy has launched “Reclaiming America First,” an initiative meant to take back that mantle from what it describes as Trump's hawkish drift, and to articulate an alternative vision for American foreign policy.

Arta Moeini, director of research at the Institute for Peace & Diplomacy and one of the project leads, laid out the parameters he believes should guide an “America First” approach during a Thursday panel marking the launch of the event: it should be neither ideological nor partisan, nor tied to any one individual; it should be grounded in realism; and it should prioritize core U.S. security interests and domestic renewal while rejecting unilateralism and nativism.

“Trump has shown himself to be at least disingenuous about using the term ‘America First,’” Moeini said during the panel, adding that part of the inspiration for the discussion was to combat “the taint of that association of ‘America First’ with this version of Trump.”

That question of who actually carries the tradition forward inevitably turned to Vance, long seen as its standard-bearer within the administration, but whose own words offer a measure of how far the movement’s foreign policy rhetoric has shifted since Trump’s return to office.

While panelists mostly agreed that an “America First” foreign policy was likely only to come from a conservative U.S. president, the group's read on Vance as the steward of that vision was more measured. Moeini said Vance would have been “smart enough not to go to war" with Iran, even if he might not be the right person to fix U.S. foreign policy in the Middle East.

Michael Brendan Dougherty, a senior writer for the National Review, offered a grimly ironic assessment of how a more realist foreign policy could take hold in a hypothetical Vance administration.

“If Vance is elected president after Donald Trump, he’s going to be looking at a munitions stockpile that is very depleted, and will be discouraging of him taking on unpredictable gambles. That’s not the way you want restraint to [be achieved], but it is the way it’s going now,” he said. “The Iran war is bringing about a humiliation of America, and that will bring along at least some restraint.”

Dougherty also pointed to the constraining effect of public opinion, saying that American opposition to war may have prevented Trump from taking even more dramatic steps in Iran, such as an invasion of Kharg Island.

There is evidence that elements of Trump’s base have turned against him as a result of this war. A recent survey from Navigator Research found that roughly 20% of Trump 2024 voters regret their decision. Among that group, almost half cited the war with Iran as the primary reason for their regret.

There were real policy disagreements over what "America First" meant. Daniel McCarthy, editor of Modern Age, warned that talk of a "multinodal" world echoes liberal internationalism and misreads an American public that is still proud of the country, while the panel also split over whether to encourage or deter a Polish or Japanese nuclear program. But all the panelists agreed that America First is a foreign policy movement that both predates and will outlive Trump.

“America First as an ordering principle of American statecraft will long outlive MAGA and the current coalitional dynamics at play surrounding the president,” Reid Smith, Vice President for Foreign Policy at Stand Together, said.
